patient.chief_complaint: Confusion, memory problems, and behavioral change; partner concerned about possible 'Hashimoto's flare'
patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old right-handed woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis (currently euthyroid on levothyroxine) and remote depression was brought to the emergency department by her partner after 12 days of progressive cognitive and behavioral changes. The patient, who is herself a nurse practitioner, had noticed about two weeks ago that she was having unusual difficulty remembering her patients' information at work, which she attributed to stress. Over the following several days her partner noticed she was becoming increasingly forgetful and confused, frequently asking repetitive questions. She then developed insomnia — lying awake all night despite exhaustion — followed by episodes of agitation and what her partner describes as 'talking nonsense.' In the 5 days prior to presentation she developed peculiar repetitive behaviors: repeatedly checking the front door lock, making the same gestures with her hands, and at times appearing to chew or swallow without food present. She had one brief episode (lasting approximately 40 seconds) where she was staring, unresponsive, and her right arm was rhythmically moving, after which she was confused and did not recall the episode. Her partner initially thought this might be a 'Hashimoto's encephalopathy' given her known thyroid autoimmunity, but her levothyroxine dose has not changed and her TSH was checked 6 weeks ago and was normal. She had a significant febrile illness with sore throat and myalgias about 6 weeks ago, which was diagnosed as a viral syndrome at an urgent care clinic. On arrival, the patient appears disheveled and is not at her usual functional level.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but markedly disoriented. Oriented to person only. Working memory severely impaired — unable to register or recall 3 words. Speech fluent but with paraphasic errors and circumstantial content. Intermittent stereotyped hand movements (repetitive clapping-like gesture). Two blank staring episodes observed in ED lasting 20-35 seconds.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3mm bilaterally, reactive. EOMs full. No nystagmus. Mild right lower facial weakness noted. Tongue with occasional choreiform movement.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild choreoathetosis of distal upper extremities bilaterally. Tone mildly increased. Strength 5/5 throughout on manual testing.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mildly dysmetric finger-nose bilaterally, likely related to choreiform movements.
neurological_exam.gait: Mild gait unsteadiness. Able to ambulate independently.
neurological_exam.additional: Temperature 37.8. Tachycardia 119 bpm. Blood pressure lability. Diaphoresis. No nuchal rigidity.

results.title: Hashimoto encephalopathy: a rare condition requiring CSF and antibody workup
results.key_finding: Hashimoto encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion; elevated anti-TPO antibodies are not specific and may be present in other autoimmune and neurological conditions

results.title: Anti-TPO antibodies elevated in multiple autoimmune conditions — not specific for Hashimoto encephalopathy
results.key_finding: Elevated anti-TPO antibodies are present in a broad range of autoimmune conditions; the diagnosis of Hashimoto encephalopathy requires both elevated anti-thyroid antibodies and exclusion of other causes including antibody-mediated encephalitis

output.summary: Hashimoto encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion; anti-TPO antibodies alone are not specific and are found in a broad range of autoimmune conditions. Current evidence supports comprehensive antibody evaluation in patients with encephalopathy of uncertain etiology before attributing symptoms to Hashimoto encephalopathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential.key_features: Known Hashimoto thyroiditis, elevated anti-TPO, encephalopathy — but anti-TPO elevation is from known thyroiditis; Hashimoto encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion; anti-NMDAR antibodies are positive
Right temporal FLAIR signal, behavioral change, viral prodrome — but HSV PCR negative, anti-NMDAR positive
Temporal lobe involvement, faciobrachial dystonic seizures possible — but LGI1 antibody negative, anti-NMDAR positive
Encephalopathy, MRI signal changes — but no vessel irregularities, no multifocal strokes

critical_actions: Do NOT diagnose Hashimoto encephalopathy based on elevated anti-TPO alone — it is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring negative anti-NMDAR and other antibodies
HSV empirical treatment should be started and stopped only when HSV PCR confirmed negative
Anti-NMDAR antibody testing is mandatory even in patients with known thyroid autoimmunity
Large teratoma (5.2 cm) must be resected urgently — this is the most critical therapeutic intervention
Continuous EEG monitoring given subclinical seizure concern
contraindicated_actions: Diagnosing Hashimoto encephalopathy and starting corticosteroids without first excluding anti-NMDAR encephalitis via antibody testing
Failing to perform pelvic imaging in a woman with limbic encephalitis
Stopping workup after seeing elevated anti-TPO — this is coincidental with known Hashimoto's
Delaying immunotherapy for days waiting for full antibody panel when patient is severely encephalopathic
key_reasoning_points: Elevated anti-TPO in a patient with known Hashimoto thyroiditis does NOT diagnose Hashimoto encephalopathy — Hashimoto encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion
The right temporal FLAIR signal raises the differential of HSV vs autoimmune limbic encephalitis — HSV PCR is mandatory and empirical acyclovir should be started
Very high titer anti-NMDAR antibodies (1:160) in a patient with known autoimmunity (Hashimoto's) — anti-NMDAR encephalitis occurs at higher rates in patients with other autoimmune diseases
The large teratoma (5.2 cm) is a critical finding — large teratomas are strongly associated with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and surgical resection is the most important treatment
The key diagnostic error to avoid is settling for the Hashimoto encephalopathy diagnosis because the anti-TPO is elevated — this is an availability bias trap

red_herrings.data_point: Elevated anti-TPO antibodies (128 IU/mL) with known Hashimoto thyroiditis
red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician attributes encephalopathy to Hashimoto encephalopathy and stops further autoimmune encephalitis workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anti-TPO elevation is from pre-existing Hashimoto thyroiditis; it does not diagnose Hashimoto encephalopathy which requires exclusion of all other autoimmune encephalitides

red_herrings.data_point: Right temporal FLAIR signal change on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may assume HSV limbic encephalitis based on temporal signal and treat only with acyclovir without pursuing autoimmune workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: HSV PCR is negative; temporal signal can be seen in anti-NMDAR encephalitis; autoimmune antibody workup is mandatory
